title: What training do crop insurance agents and loss adjusters need under the federal program?
description: Federal crop insurance training under the 2027 Standard Reinsurance Agreement: 12 and 3 hour agent rules, 60 and 16 hour adjuster rules, 3 year retests.
shortAnswer: Under Appendix IV of the Standard Reinsurance Agreement between the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation (FCIC) and approved insurance providers, administered by the USDA Risk Management Agency (RMA), a new crop insurance agent needs at least 12 hours of structured training and a competency test before selling, then 3 hours every year. A new loss adjuster needs at least 60 hours, including 24 in a classroom, then 16 hours a year. Both retest every three years.
keyTakeaways: The duty sits with the insurer: Appendix IV Section II of the 2027 Standard Reinsurance Agreement (SRA) makes each approved insurance provider (AIP) responsible for a Training and Performance Evaluation Plan and an annual report to FCIC.

New agents and anyone who solicits crop insurance sales need at least 12 hours of structured training on a set curriculum and must pass a basic competency test before selling or servicing a policy (Section II(d)(1)).
Experienced agents need at least 3 hours of structured training every year regardless of sales activity, including at least 1 hour on new products approved in the previous year.

New loss adjusters need at least 60 hours, including at least 24 classroom hours, before signing any claim; experienced adjusters need at least 16 hours a year, including 8 classroom hours (Section II(d)(2)).
All agents and loss adjusters must retake and pass the competency test every three years, and an AIP hiring someone from another AIP must document a pass within the past 3 years.
jurisdiction: United States (Federal Crop Insurance Program; 2027 Standard Reinsurance Agreement, reinsurance year beginning July 1, 2026)
regulator: USDA Risk Management Agency (RMA), which administers the program of the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation (FCIC) through approved insurance providers (AIPs); agents are also licensed by state insurance departments
appliesTo: Approved insurance providers that sign the Standard Reinsurance Agreement with FCIC
Crop insurance agents and any other individuals who solicit or promote crop insurance sales for an AIP
Loss adjusters and employees who adjust or sign claims on eligible crop insurance contracts
AIP employees performing sales, service, loss adjustment and underwriting functions

sections.heading: Where do federal crop insurance training requirements come from?

blocks.text: The training standards are contractual terms of the Standard Reinsurance Agreement (SRA), the agreement under which FCIC reinsures and subsidizes the policies that approved insurance providers sell. They are set out in [Appendix IV, Quality Assurance and Program Integrity](https://www.rma.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2026-03/SRA_AppendixIV_2027.pdf), of the 2027 SRA dated July 1, 2026, published on RMA's [reinsurance agreements page](https://www.rma.usda.gov/policy-procedure/reinsurance-agreements), as at November 2026.

The SRA runs by reinsurance year, which it defines as the term beginning July 1 and ending June 30 of the following year, named for the year containing June. The 2027 reinsurance year therefore runs from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. The [main 2027 SRA](https://www.rma.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2026-03/SRA_2027.pdf) defines an agent as an individual licensed by the state where the contracts are sold and authorized by the company to sell and service them, and a loss adjuster as an individual licensed by a state, or who has passed an FCIC-approved proficiency testing program, who verifies information and makes factual determinations on losses.

Because the obligation is placed on the AIP, an agent or adjuster meets it through the AIP's training program. State licensing rules apply separately; Florida, for example, excludes holders of a limited crop or hail and multiple-peril crop insurance agent license from its general CE statute, as noted on the page on [Florida insurance adjuster continuing education](/regulations/florida-insurance-adjuster-continuing-education).

sections.heading: How much training does a crop insurance agent need?

blocks.text: A new agent needs at least 12 hours of structured training and a passed competency test before selling or servicing any eligible crop insurance contract, and an experienced agent needs at least 3 hours every year. Section II(d)(1) of Appendix IV sets the minimums.

items: **New agents (II(d)(1)(A)):** at least 12 hours of structured training on all items in the sales curriculum. This also covers any other individual who solicits or otherwise promotes crop insurance sales on behalf of the company.

**Experienced agents (II(d)(1)(B)):** at least 3 hours of structured training each year on updates or changes, or on areas found deficient in quality control reviews. Training must be given to all applicable individuals regardless of sales activity or pay status, and must include at least 1 hour on new products if any were approved in the previous year.
**Materials currency:** training materials must be updated to include all new FCIC programs within six months of board approval.

**Competency test (II(d)(1)(C)):** all agents must pass a basic competency test tied to the curriculum before selling or servicing, and the company must review results and document follow-up training for weaknesses.

**Retesting (II(d)(1)(D) and (E)):** all agents must retake and pass the test every three years; for an agent new to the company, the AIP must obtain documentation of a pass within the past 3 years with another AIP.

blocks.text: The SRA defines an experienced agent as one who has completed at least one full year of sales and service and is current on any certifications FCIC requires.

sections.heading: What must the sales training curriculum cover?

blocks.text: The curriculum must make agents proficient in the policies, procedures and integrity rules for every contract the AIP sells in its states. New agents learn all of it; experienced agents learn updates and changes. Section II(b)(1) lists the minimum content.

items: The terms and conditions of the Common Crop Insurance Policy Basic Provisions and Crop Provisions at 7 C.F.R. part 457, and other plans of insurance, and changes to them.
Applicable endorsements, Special Provisions and options.
The benefits and differences between plans and their suitability to local farming conditions, including conservation activities and organic and sustainable practices.
The actuarial documents and their use.
Procedures for sales and service of eligible contracts.
How to complete and submit forms, documents, notices and reports.
Federal civil rights requirements and methods to encourage participation, including by underserved producers as defined by section 11108 of the Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018.
Recognizing anomalies and common indicators of misrepresentation, fraud, waste or abuse, and how to report them.
Business conduct and ethics law, including rebating prohibitions, conflicts of interest and controlled business.
Any other requirements FCIC establishes.

sections.heading: How much training does a crop insurance loss adjuster need?

blocks.text: A new loss adjuster needs at least 60 hours of structured training, including at least 24 hours in a classroom, before adjusting or signing any claim. An experienced loss adjuster needs at least 16 hours each year, including at least 8 classroom hours. Section II(d)(2) of Appendix IV sets these minimums, which are five times the agent's initial hours.

The loss adjustment curriculum in Section II(c)(1) reuses most of the sales topics, including policy terms, actuarial documents, forms, fraud indicators and ethics, and adds loss adjustment procedures, how to verify information on forms and reports, how to determine the amount of production used to calculate losses, and federal civil rights requirements. All loss adjusters must pass a basic competency test that tests their ability to determine the amount of loss accurately, and must retake and pass it every three years (II(d)(2)(C) and (D)).

An experienced loss adjuster is one who has completed at least one full year of loss adjustment and is current on FCIC certifications. Assessment design matters here because the test must show proficiency, not just attendance; the guide on [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments) covers the method.

sections.heading: What must the insurance company document?

blocks.text: Each AIP must file a Training and Performance Evaluation Plan (TPEP) with its annual Plan of Operations and an annual Training and Performance Evaluation Report (TPER). Section II(a) sets the contents.

items: **TPEP measurement standards:** acceptable standards for test proficiency and satisfactory work performance, and internal controls to track and evaluate performance against them.

**Curricula and timeline:** training for new and experienced agents and adjusters, for those with deficient performance, and for employees in sales, service, loss adjustment and underwriting, with a timeline to train everyone before the work is performed.
**Named owners and remediation:** the names of those responsible for training, and the plan for corrective action when additional training does not fix deficiencies.
**Records for FCIC:** procedures to keep and provide on request the performance history of each individual and records of all corrective actions.
**TPER:** an evaluation of each agent and loss adjuster, including a review of associated loss ratios and errors or omissions, and a report of remedial actions taken.

blocks.text: Proficiency is ongoing. Under Sections II(b)(2)(F) and (G) and II(c)(2)(F) and (G), proficiency means passing the test and maintaining satisfactory work performance during the crop year, and performance is satisfactory if reviews of producer complaints, state insurance department or FCIC inquiries, or other quality control reviews find no material errors. Section III(a)(2) requires quality control reviews to be conducted by independent individuals who were not involved in the sale or the loss adjustment reviewed.

sections.heading: What evidence would an FCIC review expect?

blocks.text: The SRA ties training to performance, so evidence must link hours and test results to each person's work record. The table maps each obligation to role, frequency and evidence.

blocks.text: Annual minimums for thousands of agents are easier to manage with a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) that tracks hours by person, contract type and crop year. State producer CE, which crop agents may also owe depending on their license, is covered on the page on [insurance producer continuing education requirements](/regulations/insurance-producer-continuing-education-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the Appendix IV sales and loss adjustment curricula as structured frameworks, with competency test items mapped to each topic. When FCIC approves a new program or changes procedures, the affected topics, materials and people are identified, which supports the six month materials update rule and the annual TPER.

faqs.q: Does an agent who sold no crop policies this year still need annual training?
faqs.a: Yes. Section II(d)(1)(B) of Appendix IV requires the annual 3 hours of structured training to be administered to all applicable individuals regardless of sales activity or pay status, so inactive agents who remain authorized must still complete it.

faqs.q: Can a loss adjuster complete all training online?
faqs.a: Not entirely. Appendix IV requires at least 24 classroom hours within the 60 hour program for new loss adjusters, and at least 8 classroom hours within the 16 annual hours for experienced loss adjusters. The remaining hours can use other structured formats the AIP's plan allows.

faqs.q: Does a competency test passed with another company count?
faqs.a: It can. For agents and loss adjusters new to an AIP, the company must obtain, and make available on request, documentation that the individual passed the basic competency test within the past 3 years with another AIP. Annual training with the new company still applies.

faqs.q: Who is responsible if an agent was not trained?
faqs.a: The approved insurance provider. Appendix IV places the training, testing and reporting obligations on the company that signs the Standard Reinsurance Agreement, and its Training and Performance Evaluation Report must evaluate each agent and loss adjuster and report remedial actions to FCIC.

factCheck.claim: 2027 SRA Appendix IV (dated 07-01-26) Section II(d)(1): new agents and others who solicit sales at least 12 hours structured training; experienced agents at least 3 hours annually regardless of sales activity or pay status, including at least 1 hour on new products approved in the previous year; materials updated within six months of board approval; competency test before selling; retest every three years; documentation of pass within past 3 years with another AIP.

2027 SRA Appendix IV Section II(d)(2): new loss adjusters at least 60 hours including at least 24 classroom hours before signing any claim; experienced loss adjusters at least 16 hours annually including at least 8 classroom hours; competency test and retest every three years.

2027 SRA Appendix IV Section II(b)(1)(A) to (J) sales curriculum, including 7 C.F.R. part 457, underserved producers under section 11108 of the Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018, fraud indicators, rebating and conflicts of interest; Section II(c)(1) loss adjustment curriculum including production determination.

2027 SRA Appendix IV Section II(a): TPEP in Plan of Operations with measurement standards, curricula, named individuals, timeline, remediation and records; annual TPER evaluating each agent and loss adjuster including loss ratios; II(b)(2)(F)-(G) and II(c)(2)(F)-(G) proficiency and satisfactory performance; Section III(a)(2) independent quality control reviewers.

2027 SRA definitions: reinsurance year begins July 1 and ends June 30 of the following year, identified by the year containing June; agent licensed by the state and authorized by the company; experienced agent and experienced loss adjuster have completed at least one full year; loss adjuster licensed by a state or passed an FCIC-approved proficiency testing program.
RMA reinsurance agreements page lists the 2027 SRA and Appendix IV documents (posted March 2026).
Florida Statutes 626.2815(2) excludes individuals holding a limited license as a crop or hail and multiple-peril crop insurance agent from the CE requirement.
